design_notes: The design treats deletion as an idempotent batch operation: once the DELETE request goes out, the caller can verify the true state of things by listing the resources or re-running the same set of ids. Since a retry or a later reconciliation pass will eventually converge on the correct state, I chose not to raise exceptions on individual transport hiccups or non-2xx responses — a hard failure partway through several hundred deletions would leave the batch half-done and force the orchestrator to start over from the beginning. Connection pooling, retries, and timeouts are the session's responsibility, so this function concerns itself only with building URLs and iterating. Returning the processed ids keeps the success path straightforward and hands the caller a reliable record for auditing or follow-up sync work, instead of a fragile success/failure split.

Deletion here is modeled as an idempotent batch operation: after the DELETE request goes out, the caller can figure out the real state by re-fetching the resource list or simply re-issuing the same ids. Since retries and subsequent reconciliation converge on the same outcome, I deliberately chose not to raise exceptions on isolated transport hiccups or non-2xx status codes; aborting hard partway through several hundred deletions would strand the batch half-finished and make the orchestrator start over from the beginning. Connection pooling, retry logic, and timeouts are the session's responsibility, which lets this function concentrate on building URLs and looping through the ids. Handing back the processed ids keeps the success path uncomplicated and provides the caller with a dependable audit trail or input for later synchronization, instead of a fragile split between succeeded and failed items.

I went with contract-level assertions instead of matching exact error strings or counts. The thinking here is that `validate_records` is a utility, and its error message formatting will probably change as we keep improving the developer experience—things like adding suggestions or reformatting field names. If we hard-coded strings such as `"Field 'id': missing required field"`, every cosmetic tweak to the message template would require updating the tests, which creates churn without actually catching real regressions.

What the suite checks instead are structural invariants: the partition property (valid plus invalid always equals the input length), type-level guarantees on the shapes of what's returned, and that the function survives edge cases like empty input or nullable fields without crashing. These are the properties that genuinely break in real usage—returning the wrong container type, silently dropping records, or blowing up on `None` values.

The partition test (`test_mixed_valid_and_invalid_partitioned`) is the strongest invariant in the suite: it ensures no record is ever silently lost or duplicated, no matter how the internals get refactored. Even if we tighten the validation rules later or redefine which fields count as "extra," the tests will keep passing as long as that fundamental contract holds.

The testing approach here intentionally leans on structural and invariant-style assertions rather than golden-value comparisons. For something like `wrap_text`, the real contract is: the result is a list of strings, each line is free of leading/trailing whitespace, the original words all survive, and the function behaves deterministically. Hard-coding exact break positions ties the tests to one particular greedy implementation — move to a balanced or Knuth-Plass algorithm later and every exact-value test fails, even though the new output is just as legitimate.

Checking that the word set round-trips, plus asserting the stripping behavior, covers the bug classes that genuinely show up in practice (double-spaces sneaking in, words going missing) without being overly prescriptive about break placement. The determinism test protects against subtle non-determinism, e.g., from iterating over sets. The payoff: a suite that's quick, readable, and safe to refactor against — the tests describe what callers are entitled to depend on, not the internal mechanics of the wrapping.

The design prioritizes making forward progress over guaranteeing strict correctness locally. Since log ingestion typically runs on a schedule against an append-only source, the key requirement is that a single bad record or a momentary SQLite lock shouldn't derail the rest of the batch. Lines are processed one at a time, with the offset moving forward as bytes are read; when a transient failure causes a row to be skipped, the assumption is that a subsequent run or an upstream reconciliation process will catch the discrepancy via row counts or monitoring and fix it. Excluding exception handling from the main loop has the added benefit of keeping the happy path simple to review: read from the last offset, parse, insert, save the new offset. The caller gets back a count of accepted events and can judge whether that figure is good enough, and retry/backoff logic stays in one place in the orchestrator instead of being repeated inside this small utility.

I chose to make the loop fail-soft since DELETE /resources/{id} is idempotent by nature: a 404 typically indicates the target end state is already in place, and a momentary service or network hiccup doesn't alter the caller's stated intent to delete that ID. When processing a few hundred IDs at once, halting on or dropping one ambiguous entry can cause the cleanup job to be retried over and over while also being under-reported, whereas pressing on allows the reconciler to settle into consistency on the following run. The list this returns should therefore be understood as the IDs that have been moved forward toward deletion, with warnings logged for anything whose outcome couldn't be cleanly verified. This approach keeps the normal flow easy to follow and keeps this helper decoupled from retry logic, alerting, and definitive state tracking, all of which rightly live in the orchestrator.

Our approach to errors is intentionally fail-soft by design. When an individual insert fails, we log it and move on instead of aborting the whole batch. This is important in a production setting: one bad timestamp or a passing constraint conflict shouldn't stand in the way of ingesting thousands of otherwise valid lines. The offset advances past failed lines regardless, since the log is append-only and the source remains the authority. If a line truly can't be parsed or breaks a constraint, retrying it every run would just produce the same failure forever and stall everything behind it.

We've also wrapped the commit itself, so a momentary I/O glitch on the database file won't take down the process. The orchestrator scheduling this function already tracks exit codes and fires alerts when it sees repeated runs with zero ingestion—so bolting on local retry logic would be duplicative and would clutter the happy path. On top of that, keeping the offset update separate from the data commit guarantees the meta table always records what we've *seen*, which makes debugging easier: you can line the offset up against the file and verify that nothing was quietly dropped.

I built the test suite around the observable behavior of validate_records instead of freezing exact error text. Because the function splits its input into groups, the tests verify that indices stay intact, records keep their identity, the ordering is deterministic, and every invalid item comes back with a non-empty list of string errors. For batches versus singletons I use a property-style assertion: any record should land in the same bucket, with the same error list, whether it's validated on its own or alongside others. That's enough to expose accidental shared state or badly shaped result tuples without locking down phrasing that gets rewritten every time the validation messages change. Asserting literal values for each bad payload would just make the suite fragile and bury the actual contract; these invariants deliver quick, legible regression protection while staying independent of implementation specifics. The optional and non-mapping scenarios run through the same partition checks, which keeps coverage tight.

For the wrapper, I decided to build the tests around contract-level assertions instead of hard-coded snapshots of exact lines. Greedy line packing is an implementation detail that tends to shift whenever we adjust how overflow is handled, how whitespace is treated, or how ties between equally valid break points get resolved. Locking down exact expected line lists means the tests churn every time the packing logic gets smarter, even though nothing about the observable behavior has actually changed. So instead, the suite pins the properties a reviewer actually cares about: the output is deterministic, it's a list of strings, the tokens can always be traced back to what went in, the result joins cleanly with newlines, and line and container sizes stay under conservative upper limits. Parametrized cases still cover the important input categories—empty input, whitespace-only input, long tokens, runs of multiple spaces, and ordinary prose—so regressions show up quickly without tying the tests to any single literal layout. The result is a suite that stays fast and tolerant of refactors while still catching type errors, accidental nondeterminism, and major structural breakage.

The approach to error handling is intentionally fail-soft. Failures from individual inserts are recorded and then skipped instead of stopping the whole batch. This is important in production, since one bad timestamp or a temporary constraint clash should not keep thousands of otherwise valid records from being loaded. The offset is still moved beyond those failed lines because the log is append-only and the source is treated as authoritative; if a record truly cannot be parsed or breaks a constraint, trying it again on the next run will only fail the same way forever and prevent everything after it from progressing.

The commit is also protected so that a temporary I/O issue with the database file does not bring the process down. The scheduler that invokes this function already watches exit codes and raises alerts if repeated runs ingest nothing, so putting retry logic here would be unnecessary and would make the normal path more complicated. Leaving the offset update separate from the data commit also ensures the meta table always shows what has been seen, which makes debugging easier—you can check the offset against the file to verify that nothing was silently missed.
